concept.name: Producer price index
concept.definition: A family of indexes published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics measuring the average change over time in selling prices received by domestic producers of goods and services. It measures price change from the seller's perspective, in contrast to the CPI's purchaser perspective.
concept.intuition: PPI tracks what producers charge at the factory gate or for their services; because it captures price pressure before the retail level, traders watch it as a possible early signal of consumer inflation.
concept.mechanics: BLS surveys over 16,000 establishments for roughly 64,000 price quotes per month and publishes indexes by industry, by commodity, and by the Final Demand-Intermediate Demand (FD-ID) system, which groups goods, services, and construction by buyer type and processing stage. Weights come from value-of-shipments data in the economic censuses.
concept.formula: PPI percent change = (PPI_t / PPI_{t-1} - 1) x 100 for a given index; indexes are weighted averages of establishment price relatives.
concept.failure_modes: PPI excludes most imports and part of the service sector, margins between producer and consumer prices vary, and pass-through to CPI is incomplete and lagged, so PPI spikes do not map one-for-one into consumer inflation.
concept.misconceptions: PPI is not a direct predictor of next month's CPI; sellers' and purchasers' prices differ due to taxes, subsidies, and distribution costs, and many services in CPI have no PPI counterpart.
concept.example: When the PPI for final demand jumped in early 2021-2022 amid supply bottlenecks, analysts read it as pipeline pressure that preceded the broader CPI surge.

citations.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Producer Price Indexes Overview
